title: Lesson 7: Appropriate Communication in Staff WhatsApp Groups
summary: A staff WhatsApp group is a professional channel. The same respect, confidentiality and clarity expected in person also apply to digital messages.

items.label: Focus
items.body: Digital professionalism, workplace etiquette, clarity, confidentiality, accountability and respectful communication

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a supervisor sends an important message to the Zura Spa staff WhatsApp group.
The message explains that a particular treatment room will be unavailable for several hours because maintenance work is scheduled.
However, some employees do not read the message carefully.
Others respond with unrelated jokes and stickers.
A few employees begin discussing personal matters, causing the important announcement to disappear among many unrelated messages.
Later, a therapist prepares the room without knowing that maintenance is scheduled.
The situation creates confusion and delays.
Now imagine the same message being handled differently.
The supervisor communicates the update clearly.
Employees read the message, ask relevant questions and acknowledge the information where required.
The group remains organised, and everyone understands the operational change.
A workplace WhatsApp group is not simply a place where employees exchange messages. It is a professional communication channel that supports coordination, accountability and teamwork.
At Zura Spa, employees must understand that the same standards of respect, confidentiality and professionalism expected during face-to-face interactions also apply to digital communication.

sections.title: 2. What is a staff WhatsApp group?
paragraphs: A staff WhatsApp group is a communication platform used by employees and management to exchange information related to workplace operations.
The purpose of the group should be clearly understood by its members.
The fact that a WhatsApp group feels informal does not make its workplace communication informal or consequence-free.
list: Work schedules and shift updates.
Important announcements.
Appointment-related coordination.
Operational instructions.
Training information.
Meeting reminders.
General workplace updates.
Task assignments and confirmations.
Approved requests for assistance.
Information that is relevant to the staff members included in the group.

sections.title: 1. It improves communication
paragraphs: Important information can reach relevant employees efficiently.

sections.title: 2. It supports teamwork
paragraphs: Employees can coordinate responsibilities and communicate operational changes.

sections.title: 3. It reduces misunderstandings
paragraphs: Clear messages help employees understand instructions, deadlines and expectations.

sections.title: 4. It protects professionalism
paragraphs: Respectful communication reduces unnecessary conflict, gossip and embarrassment.

sections.title: 5. It protects confidentiality
paragraphs: Employees are reminded to handle private information carefully and avoid unnecessary disclosures.

sections.title: 6. It saves time
paragraphs: Organised communication reduces repeated questions and unnecessary messages.

sections.title: 4. The difference between personal and professional WhatsApp communication
paragraphs: Employees may use WhatsApp casually with friends and family.
However, workplace groups require a different approach.
Employees do not need to sound excessively formal in every message.
However, they should communicate in a way that reflects the purpose of the group.

sections.title: 5. Ten rules for appropriate communication in staff WhatsApp groups
Rule 1: Keep messages relevant
paragraphs: Messages should relate to the purpose of the group.
Avoid unnecessary discussions that distract employees from important information.
Appropriate: "Good afternoon. Please, the 4 p.m. client has requested a change to the appointment time. Reception will confirm the updated schedule."
Inappropriate: Posting unrelated videos, jokes or forwarded messages in the middle of operational discussions.

sections.title: Rule 2: Use respectful language
paragraphs: Employees should communicate politely with colleagues, supervisors and management.
Avoid insults, mockery, sarcasm intended to humiliate and aggressive expressions.
Instead of: "Why can't you people ever do anything properly?"
Say: "Please, can we confirm the correct procedure so the issue does not happen again?"

sections.title: Rule 3: Read messages carefully before responding
paragraphs: Do not reply based on incomplete understanding.
Read the full message and any relevant earlier information.
If something is unclear, ask a specific question.

sections.title: Rule 4: Avoid unnecessary messages
paragraphs: Repeated messages, unrelated comments and excessive reactions can make important information difficult to find.
Keep responses concise and relevant.

sections.title: Rule 5: Protect confidential information
paragraphs: Do not share private client records, employee information, screenshots or sensitive business details in a general group unless there is a legitimate need and the group is authorised for that information.
Use an approved private channel when necessary.

sections.title: Rule 6: Avoid public arguments
paragraphs: A staff WhatsApp group is generally not the appropriate place for extended personal disagreements.
If a discussion becomes tense, move it to an appropriate private conversation or involve a supervisor.

sections.title: Rule 7: Acknowledge important instructions appropriately
paragraphs: When confirmation is required, respond clearly.
Examples: "Received, thank you." "Understood. I'll complete the task before 3 p.m." "Noted. I'll update reception when the room is ready."
Acknowledgment should not be mistaken for completion. Employees must still carry out the instruction and report the outcome where required.

sections.title: Rule 8: Communicate at appropriate times
paragraphs: Respect employees' working hours and agreed communication expectations.
Not every message requires an immediate response outside working hours.
Urgent matters should follow Zura Spa's established emergency or escalation arrangements rather than relying only on a group message.

sections.title: Rule 9: Verify information before sharing
paragraphs: Do not circulate rumours, assumptions or unconfirmed information as facts.
If information is uncertain, clarify it before posting.

sections.title: Rule 10: Take responsibility for your messages
paragraphs: Before sending, consider whether the message is accurate, respectful, necessary and appropriate for the audience.
If you make a mistake, correct it promptly.

sections.title: 6. How to write clear workplace WhatsApp messages
paragraphs: A professional message should be easy to understand.
list: Purpose: Why are you sending the message?
Details: What information does the team need?
Responsibility: Who needs to act?
Timing: When is action required?
Confirmation: Is an acknowledgment or update needed?

sections.title: Example — unclear versus improved
paragraphs: Unclear message: "Room issue. Somebody should check."
This message does not explain the problem or identify who should respond.

Improved message: "Good afternoon. The air conditioner in Room 2 is not cooling properly. The room is scheduled for a 3 p.m. appointment. Please, can the supervisor advise whether we should use another room?"
The second message is more useful because it provides relevant information and requests appropriate action.

sections.title: 7. Using tone appropriately in written messages
paragraphs: Unlike face-to-face communication, WhatsApp messages do not always communicate tone clearly.
A message may sound harsher than intended.
Example: "COME HERE NOW!" The use of capital letters and an abrupt command may be interpreted as shouting.
A more professional message would be: "Please, could you come to reception when you are available? We need to clarify an appointment."
Employees should avoid assuming that every brief message is rude, but they should also consider how their own words may be interpreted.
A useful habit is to reread your message before sending it, especially when you are upset.

sections.title: Common sources of misunderstanding
list: Writing entire messages in capital letters.
Using repeated exclamation marks.
Sending short replies that appear dismissive.
Using sarcasm without context.
Sending emotionally charged messages immediately.
Using ambiguous emojis or reactions.

sections.title: 8. Emojis, stickers, GIFs and voice notes
paragraphs: WhatsApp allows many forms of communication.
These features are not automatically inappropriate, but they should be used thoughtfully in workplace groups.
Lesson: The convenience of digital tools does not remove the responsibility to communicate professionally.

items.label: Emojis
items.body: A simple acknowledgment emoji may be acceptable where the group permits it. However, emojis should not replace clear responses when an instruction requires specific confirmation.

items.label: Stickers and GIFs
items.body: Avoid using stickers or GIFs to mock colleagues, dismiss concerns or interrupt serious discussions.

items.label: Voice notes
items.body: Voice notes can be useful when a spoken explanation is easier than typing. However, they should be reasonably concise and used when appropriate. For urgent instructions or information that must be referred to later, a clear written summary may be more practical.

items.label: Photos and videos
items.body: Only share images or recordings that are relevant, authorised and appropriate. Client images, treatment-room recordings or sensitive workplace materials require particular care.

sections.title: 9. Handling disagreements in staff WhatsApp groups
paragraphs: Disagreements may arise when employees interpret instructions differently or have concerns about decisions.
However, the group should not become a place for insults, personal attacks or public humiliation.
If the issue becomes personal or requires a sensitive discussion, it should be moved to an appropriate private channel.
Key principle: Resolve the issue without turning the group into an audience for conflict.

sections.title: Inappropriate exchange
paragraphs: Employee A: "You didn't prepare the room properly."
Employee B: "You're always looking for someone to blame."
Employee A: "Everybody knows how careless you are."
The conversation has moved away from resolving the problem.

sections.title: Professional exchange
paragraphs: Employee A: "I noticed Room 2 was missing clean towels before the appointment."
Employee B: "Thank you for pointing that out. I was waiting for the replacement towels. I've informed the supervisor."
Employee A: "Understood. Let's confirm the next step so the room can be ready."

sections.title: 10. Confidentiality and screenshots
paragraphs: Employees should be especially careful with screenshots, forwarded messages and copied conversations.
If a screenshot is necessary for a legitimate report, share it through the appropriate authorised channel rather than circulating it widely.
Confidentiality should not prevent lawful reporting or preservation of relevant evidence of misconduct.

sections.title: Examples of inappropriate conduct
list: Forwarding internal staff conversations to outsiders without authorisation.
Sharing private employee messages in the general group to embarrass someone.
Posting client telephone numbers unnecessarily.
Circulating screenshots of confidential booking or payment information.
Sharing sensitive internal decisions before authorised communication.

sections.title: Before sharing a screenshot, ask
list: Is there a legitimate work-related reason?
Am I authorised to share this information?
Does the recipient need to see it?
Does the screenshot contain private details that should be removed?
Is there a more appropriate channel?

sections.title: 11. Responding to instructions and announcements
paragraphs: Employees should understand the difference between receiving information and being assigned responsibility.

items.label: Informational announcement
items.body: "Tomorrow's training session begins at 9 a.m." If acknowledgment is required, employees should confirm receipt.

items.label: Task assignment
items.body: "Please ensure Room 1 is ready before the 2 p.m. appointment." The responsible employee should confirm understanding and complete the task.

items.label: Request for an update
items.body: "Please confirm whether the afternoon appointments have been finalised." The employee should provide an accurate status.

sections.title: Example of a good response
paragraphs: "Good afternoon. The 2 p.m. and 3 p.m. appointments have been confirmed. We are still awaiting confirmation for the 4 p.m. appointment. I will update the group when the client responds."
This response is more useful than simply saying: "Working on it."

sections.title: 12. When not to use the general staff WhatsApp group
paragraphs: Some matters are better handled privately or through a designated reporting channel.
A staff group may be useful for coordinating an operational response, but sensitive details should be limited to those who need them.
table: Respectful private discussion or supervisor support
Private discussion with the appropriate person
Immediate appropriate safety action and emergency communication

sections.title: 13. The THINK method before sending a message

items.label: T — True
items.body: Is the information accurate and verified?

items.label: H — Helpful
items.body: Does the message contribute to workplace coordination or problem-solving?

items.label: I — Important
items.body: Is this information relevant to the group and its purpose?

items.label: N — Necessary
items.body: Does this need to be shared with everyone, or should it go to a specific person?

items.label: K — Kind
items.body: Is the wording respectful and professional?

sections.title: THINK example
paragraphs: An employee is upset because she believes another colleague ignored an instruction.
She prepares a message: "Some people in this place are so irresponsible. They never do their work."
Before sending, she applies the THINK method.
She realises the message contains an unverified accusation, is unlikely to solve the problem and may embarrass someone.
Instead, she contacts the appropriate person: "Please, can we confirm who was assigned to prepare Room 2? The room is not ready, and the next appointment is approaching."
The revised message is more professional and solution-focused.

sections.title: Case study A: The unnecessary jokes
paragraphs: A supervisor posts an important schedule update.
Several employees respond with unrelated stickers, jokes and videos.
The important information becomes difficult to find.
Expected lesson: Workplace groups should remain focused on relevant communication.
list: Why is this behaviour inappropriate?
How could it affect operations?
What should employees do instead?
How can the group remain friendly without becoming disorganised?

sections.title: Case study B: The public argument
paragraphs: Two employees disagree about who was responsible for preparing a treatment room.
They begin exchanging angry messages in the staff group.
Other employees join the argument.
Expected lesson: Disagreements should be handled respectfully and through appropriate channels.
list: What communication mistakes occurred?
Why is a public argument harmful?
How could the employees address the issue professionally?
When should a supervisor become involved?

sections.title: Case study C: The forwarded screenshot
paragraphs: An employee forwards a screenshot from the staff group to someone outside Zura Spa.
The screenshot contains internal operational information.
Expected lesson: Employees should not forward workplace information without a legitimate reason and appropriate authorisation.
list: What confidentiality concerns arise?
Why might forwarding internal messages be inappropriate?
What should the employee have considered?
What should happen if sensitive information has already been shared?

sections.title: Case study D: The misunderstood instruction
paragraphs: A supervisor posts: "Please ensure the rooms are ready before the afternoon appointments."
An employee replies: "Noted."
However, she assumes another colleague will handle the task.
The rooms are not ready on time.
Expected lesson: Digital instructions should identify responsibilities clearly, and employees should confirm unclear assignments.
list: What was unclear about the instruction?
What should the supervisor have specified?
What should the employee have asked?
Why is acknowledgment different from task completion?

sections.title: 15. Practical group activity: Rewrite the message
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees practise turning unprofessional messages into clear, respectful workplace communication.
Expected outcome: Participants should understand how wording affects professionalism and cooperation.

sections.title: Instructions
paragraphs: Divide participants into small groups. Ask each group to rewrite the following messages.
list: WHOEVER USED ROOM 3 SHOULD GO AND CLEAN IT NOW!!!
You people never listen. I'm tired of repeating myself.
The client is angry. Somebody should do something.
Why is nobody responding? Are you all sleeping?

sections.title: Suggested improvements
table: Please, can the staff member assigned to Room 3 confirm whether cleaning has been completed?
Please review the earlier instruction and let me know if any part requires clarification.
A client has raised a concern about her appointment. Please, can the responsible supervisor assist?
Please, could the responsible person confirm receipt of the earlier message when available?

sections.title: 16. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 7 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the primary purpose of a staff WhatsApp group? Sharing unrelated entertainment throughout the day / Supporting relevant workplace communication and coordination / Discussing private matters about colleagues

A supervisor posts an important instruction. What should an employee do? Read it carefully, clarify unclear details and acknowledge when required / Respond with unrelated stickers / Assume someone else will handle it

Two employees begin arguing in the staff group. What is the most professional response? Encourage other employees to take sides / Share screenshots outside the organisation / Move the sensitive disagreement to an appropriate private discussion or supervisor

Which message is most professional? YOU PEOPLE ARE ALWAYS CARELESS!!! / Please, can we confirm who is responsible for preparing Room 2 before the next appointment? / Nobody here knows what they're doing.

What does the THINK method encourage? Checking that messages are true, helpful, important, necessary and kind / Sending messages immediately whenever upset / Sharing every concern with the entire group

sections.title: 17. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain why professional communication is important in staff WhatsApp groups.
Identify five examples of inappropriate WhatsApp group behaviour.
Describe how employees should respond to important workplace instructions.
Explain why public arguments should be avoided in staff groups.
Describe three ways employees can protect confidentiality on WhatsApp.
Rewrite three unprofessional workplace messages into respectful alternatives.
Explain the THINK method in your own words.
Describe how you would respond if you received an unclear instruction in the staff group.
Identify three personal habits you intend to improve in workplace digital communication.

sections.title: 18. Seven-day WhatsApp professionalism challenge
table: Read workplace messages carefully before responding
Keep contributions relevant to the group's purpose
Use respectful language in every work-related message
Avoid unnecessary forwarding of screenshots or private information
Resolve sensitive disagreements through appropriate channels
Review your messages and identify opportunities for improvement

sections.title: 19. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Professional communication does not end when employees leave a face-to-face conversation.
The way employees communicate through WhatsApp also reflects their professionalism, respect for colleagues and commitment to teamwork.
At Zura Spa, staff WhatsApp groups should support clear instructions, useful updates, responsible coordination and appropriate problem-solving.
Employees should avoid unnecessary distractions, public arguments, gossip, disrespectful language and unauthorised disclosure of information.

This completes Day 3: Effective Communication and Active Listening. Next: Day 4 — Emotional Intelligence, Humility and Accepting Corrections, beginning with Understanding Emotions and Emotional Triggers.

remember: Every message you send contributes to the workplace culture. Before posting, consider whether your words are accurate, necessary, respectful and appropriate for the people receiving them. Use staff WhatsApp groups to improve communication, strengthen teamwork and support the smooth operation of Zura Spa—not to create confusion, conflict or unnecessary distractions.
